title: Deny (not auto-approve) bash critical-pattern commands under yolo mode
wave: Wave 2 (Correctness trên các đường đang ship) — gated by PRODUCT SIGN-OFF, must not gate W4/W12/W13
one_line: Two one-line edits make `rm -rf /`-class bash commands resolve to `policy: "deny"` in every approval mode — including the default `yolo` — instead of silently self-approving on install.
user_visible_effect: With the default `tools.approvalMode: yolo`, a command matching `CRITICAL_BASH_PATTERNS` (`rm -rf /`, `rm --no-preserve-root`, `sudo rm`, `chmod -R 777 /`, fork bomb, `mkfs`, `dd of=/dev/`, `> /etc/passwd`, shutdown, etc.) is now refused with `Tool "bash" is blocked by tool policy. Reason: Critical pattern detected` instead of running unattended. A second, larger effect: a `bash.patterns` rule with `approval: "allow"` can NO LONGER permit a critical command — the tool deny is absolute and beats user allow. Any user whose workflow depends on `rm -rf /tmp/...` (which matches the `/`-anchored critical regex) being auto-allowed in yolo loses that, and there is no settings-level escape hatch short of editing code. This is a default-behavior change for every yolo user and is exactly why sign-off is required.

steps.instruction: GATE — do not write a line of code until a product owner signs off in writing on the exact user-visible change recorded in `user_visible_effect` above, specifically: (a) critical bash commands are now hard-denied in yolo, and (b) `bash.patterns` `allow` can no longer override a critical match. If sign-off is withheld or deferred, close this item as 'deferred' and ship Wave 2 without it (W4/W12/W13 must not wait).

In `bash.ts`, change line 516 from `return { tier: "exec", override: true, reason: "Critical pattern detected" };` to a multi-line object literal that adds `policy: "deny",` between `override: true,` and `reason:`, matching the field order used by the adjacent deny branch at lines 507-511 (`tier`, `override`, `policy`, `reason`).

In the SAME file, make the identical change at line 545 (the per-segment compound loop). Do not skip it: the top-level check at 515 is guarded by `!compoundSegments`, so every compound command reaches line 545 instead — line 545 is the branch a real compound payload such as `pwd && cmp a b && rm -rf /` actually takes. Missing one of the two sites is the single most likely way to ship this half-done.

Update `classifies critical bash patterns through BashTool.approval`: change the `toEqual` at line 371 to expect `{ tier: "exec", override: true, policy: "deny", reason: "Critical pattern detected" }`. Leave the command list above it untouched — it is the false-positive regression corpus and every entry must still be classified as critical.

Rename the it() at line 426 (currently "keeps critical bash patterns prompt-gated unless explicitly denied" — no longer true) to describe the new contract, e.g. "denies critical bash patterns even when a configured pattern allows", and add `policy: "deny"` to the expected object at lines 431-435. Keep the two sibling assertions in that same test unchanged: `echo hello` under the `*`/allow rule must still be `{tier:"write",policy:"allow"}` and `echo hello && rm file.txt` must still be `"exec"` — they are the proof the change did not overreach.

In `does not let an unmatched segment conceal a critical later segment`, change the `toMatchObject` at lines 818-822 from `policy: "prompt"` to `policy: "deny"`. It asserts in `write` mode (not yolo) — it breaks anyway because `resolveApproval` short-circuits on `decision.policy === "deny"` before mode is ever consulted.

In `retains critical checks after removing literal shell quotes and escapes with an unmatched segment`, change the `toMatchObject` at lines 834-838 from `policy: "prompt"` to `policy: "deny"`. Both loop commands (`rm -rf '/'` and `r\m -rf /`) must still be denied, proving quote-stripping/canonicalization still surfaces the critical match.

Add a new test in the same `describe("tool-owned dynamic approval declarations")` block, after the one from step 4, that drives the REAL `BashTool` (use the existing `createBashTool()` helper) and asserts the compound path under yolo: `resolveApproval(bash, { command: "pwd && cmp before after && rm -rf /" }, "yolo", { bash: "allow" })` matches `{ policy: "deny", source: "tool", override: true }`, and `requiresApproval(bash, { command: "rm -rf /" }, "yolo", { bash: "allow" })` throws a message starting `Tool "bash" is blocked by tool policy`. This is the headline contract and it must exercise the compound loop at line 545, not just the top-level branch at line 516.

Add a negative test in the same block: a harmless command under the default yolo mode still resolves `allow`. `resolveApproval(createBashTool(), { command: "ls -la" }, "yolo", {})` must match `{ policy: "allow" }`, and the existing `does not flag benign bash commands` test (line 375) must stay green. This is the guard against the change widening into ordinary commands.

Edit `docs/approval-mode.md` line 64: delete the clause "In `yolo`, a bare critical override is ignored, but an explicit tool/user `prompt` or `deny` policy is still enforced." and replace it with a statement that a critical bash pattern is refused outright in every mode, including `yolo`, and that a `bash.patterns` `allow` rule does not override it (a configured `deny` rule is still the way to name the specific pattern in the reason).

Edit the extension example at `docs/approval-mode.md:124` so the `isCritical(args.command)` branch returns the same shape the shipped bash tool now uses (include `policy: "deny"`), and add one clause noting that an `override: true` decision with no `policy` is ignored under `yolo`. Only the example text changes — the example is illustrative, not compiled.
Add the changelog bullet under `## [Unreleased]` in `packages/coding-agent/CHANGELOG.md` (create the `### Changed` subsection if absent). One line, user-facing, no implementation narration.

Run the verification commands. `bun test packages/coding-agent/test/tools/approval.test.ts` must be green with 0 failures. NOTE: in this checkout `node_modules/` is empty, so BOTH `bun test` and `bun run check:ts` currently fail before running any test — run `bun install` first (see open_questions).

test_contract: The contract defended: **a command matching `CRITICAL_BASH_PATTERNS` is never self-approved by `yolo` — it resolves `policy: "deny"` with `source: "tool"` and `requiresApproval` throws, in every mode, through BOTH the top-level branch and the per-segment compound branch.** Consumer-visible regression if it breaks: `rm -rf /` (or `pwd && cmp a b && rm -rf /`) silently executes unattended under the default approval mode on a developer's machine — silent data loss, no prompt, no log line, and nothing in the transcript says the safety classifier fired. The negative half is equally load-bearing: if the change over-reaches, an ordinary `ls -la` stops resolving to `allow` in yolo and every automation built on the default mode breaks loudly. The step-5 sibling assertions (`echo hello` still `write`/`allow`, `echo hello && rm file.txt` still `"exec"`) are the second negative guard, proving the deny did not leak into the configured-pattern resolution order.

Equivalently: reverting either of the two `bash.ts` edits without reverting the tests turns the suite red.
effort: S — two one-line source edits, five test-assertion updates, two new tests, two doc edits, one changelog line.
risk: **Half-applying the pair.** The top-level check at `bash.ts:515` is guarded by `!compoundSegments`, so it is unreachable for every compound command; line 545 is the branch a real payload actually reaches. Fixing 516 alone produces tests that pass (the top-level corpus is large) while `pwd && cmp a b && rm -rf /` still self-approves in yolo — the exact silent-failure the item exists to prevent. Second-highest risk: the sign-off gate being treated as advisory. This changes default behavior for every yolo user and removes the `bash.patterns` allow escape hatch, so implementing it without a recorded sign-off is itself the failure — mark it skipped and ship Wave 2 without it rather than guessing.
open_questions: SIGN-OFF (hard gate): does product accept that `bash.patterns` `{ approval: "allow" }` can no longer permit ANY command matching `CRITICAL_BASH_PATTERNS`? This is the sharpest part of the change and the plan does not call it out. `rm -rf /tmp/build` matches the `/`-anchored recursive-delete regex, so users who currently rely on an allow rule to auto-run cleanup in yolo lose it with no settings-level escape hatch. Options: (a) ship as-is (recommended — a safety classifier with a documented opt-out is not a safety classifier); (b) make the critical deny yield to an explicit user `tools.approval.bash: "allow"` (weakens the gate, and contradicts the adjacent deny branch's own precedence); (c) narrow `CRITICAL_BASH_PATTERNS` so `/tmp` and `/var/tmp` are excluded. Recommend (a) and ask the owner to confirm explicitly.

The plan instructs: rename the existing test at `approval.test.ts:84` ("ignores override-based prompts in yolo mode") to describe the new behavior. Verification says that instruction is wrong. That test's input is a synthetic object built inline at line 82 (`const dangerous = tool("bash", { tier: "exec", override: true, reason: "Critical pattern detected" })`) — it never calls BashTool, so it still passes unchanged after the bash.ts edit, and renaming it would assert something false. The spec keeps it as-is (it still guards a genuinely reachable shape: any tool returning `override:true` with no `policy`) and adds the real-BashTool test at step 8. Confirm this deviation is acceptable, or direct otherwise.

Is `policy: "prompt"` acceptable as an alternative to `deny`? Under yolo, a tool decision carrying an explicit `policy` is returned verbatim with `override: false` (approval.ts yolo branch), so a critical command would prompt instead of being refused. It was rejected in favor of `deny` because `docs/approval-mode.md:162` documents that a `prompt` policy is unsatisfiable in a headless subagent, and ACP/headless sessions would fail inconsistently; `deny` fails closed deterministically. Confirm `deny` is the intent before implementing — this is not a detail the engineer should decide.

Should `docs/approval-mode.md:124`'s extension-authoring example be changed to the new shape, or left as a demonstration that a bare override is still legal but yolo-ignored? The spec changes it (step 11) on the grounds that it currently teaches extension authors a shape that silently does nothing under the default mode.
